newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany welcomes defence dialogue with France.
newsitem.headline: Germany welcomes defence dialogue with France.

text.p: Germany has responded favourably to France's offer to hold a dialogue on nuclear deterrence in a European defence policy and to consult on interventions in international crises, government and opposition leaders said.

A high government official said late on Monday there was nothing secret about an agreement on a common strategic concept adopted by Germany and France last month, but not made public until it was leaked last week in the French newspaper Le Monde.

He said the 12-page document, which was due for publication later this week in any case, was nothing more than a pledge by the two countries to discuss ways to cooperate more closely on defence in the context of France's rapprochement with NATO.
"I believe it is a good thing," said the official, who spoke on the condition he not be named.
No decisions other than a commitment to discuss issues had been made, he said. It was wrong to read into the paper a French effort to divide the Atlantic Alliance, he added.

The agreements were contained in a common strategic concept adopted by Germany and France at a summit in Nuremberg last month. Le Monde published what it said were excerpts from the German text of the document.

The French Foreign Ministry issued a statement later on Friday that the two governments had agreed to make the agreement public, probably on January 30, after releasing it to their parliaments and their NATO and European Union partners.
A leader of the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) said he had not yet seen the document, but welcomed the basic idea that Europe's defence was developing its own identity.

"I consider the basic idea that the European Union develops a defence identity of its own and has its own instruments to be the right thing," Guenter Verheugen, vice chairman of the SPD in parliament, said during a speech to journalists.

After an international furore over French nuclear testing in 1995, French Prime Minister Alain Juppe called for discussion of a policy of "concerted deterrence" which implied Paris might consult its European allies in widening the definition of vital interests covered by its deterrent.
Germany renounced nuclear weapons after World War Two and accepted U.S. nuclear weapons on its soil under NATO.
France's atomic arsenal has long given it the upper hand in defence and foreign policy discussions with Bonn.
While nothing in the document bars France from unilateral military actions, both countries agreed "to consult about an intervention aimed at preventing or settling a crisis".

"All our conventional forces, including rapid reaction forces, are primarily at the service of the defence of our allies in the framework of obligations resulting from the Brussels and Washington treaties," it said, referring to the founding agreements of the Western European Union and NATO.
